arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Carter Phillips argued the case involves findings the common law never entrusted to juries.
The government advocate stated the judge decides how often the crime was committed for sentencing.
Justice Alito questioned whether a corporation has a Sixth Amendment right to a jury trial.
Justice Kennedy asked what standard applies to jury trials when fines are involved.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: Southern Union Company faces federal charges for violating a law over several months. The government sought a fine based on the number of days of violation. A lower court judge determined the duration and set the fine. The company argues this fact belongs to the jury. The government argues the judge may decide sentencing facts.

paragraphs: The company wants the jury to decide the number of violation days.
The government wants the judge to determine the duration for sentencing.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The company argues the duration is an element of the offense requiring a jury verdict.
The government argues the duration is a sentencing fact traditionally decided by judges.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the boundary between jury and judge roles in corporate criminal sentencing. It determines who controls the calculation of fines based on offense duration. The outcome shapes the procedural rights of corporations facing federal charges. It clarifies the scope of the Sixth Amendment in white-collar crime cases.
